name.text: Application of scale factors to a cylindrical model (revised)

questiontext.text:
An engineering firm has designed a prototype for a chemical storage tank. The prototype consists of a cylindrical body with a hemispherical top, with the dimensions shown in the diagram below.

The firm decides to produce an industrial version of the tank by enlarging every dimension by a linear scale factor of \(k = {@k@}\).

[[jsxgraph width="350px" height="400px"]] var board = JXG.JSXGraph.initBoard(divid, { boundingbox: [-10, 20, 10, -5], axis: false, showCopyright: false, pan: {enabled: false}, zoom: {enabled: false} }); var R = {#r_p#} * 1.5; var H = {#h_p#} * 1.5; var p = 0.3; /* ===================== HEMISPHERICAL TOP ===================== */ // top visible arc board.create('curve', [ function(t){return R*Math.cos(t)}, function(t){return H + R*Math.sin(t)}, 0, Math.PI ], { strokeColor: '#1f77b4', strokeWidth: 3, fixed: true, highlight: false }); // bottom hidden arc board.create('curve', [ function(t){return R*Math.cos(t)}, function(t){return H + (R*p)*Math.sin(t)}, Math.PI, 2*Math.PI ], { strokeColor: '#1f77b4', dash: 2, strokeWidth: 2, fixed: true, highlight: false }); /* ===================== CYLINDER SIDES ===================== */ board.create('segment', [[-R,0],[-R,H]], { strokeColor:'#2ca02c', strokeWidth:3, fixed: true, highlight: false }); board.create('segment', [[R,0],[R,H]], { strokeColor:'#2ca02c', strokeWidth:3, fixed: true, highlight: false }); /* ===================== CYLINDER BASE ===================== */ // visible base board.create('curve', [ function(t){return R*Math.cos(t)}, function(t){return (R*p)*Math.sin(t)}, Math.PI,2*Math.PI ], { strokeColor:'#2ca02c', strokeWidth:3, fixed: true, highlight: false }); // hidden base board.create('curve', [ function(t){return R*Math.cos(t)}, function(t){return (R*p)*Math.sin(t)}, 0,Math.PI ], { strokeColor:'#2ca02c', dash:2, strokeWidth:2, fixed: true, highlight: false }); /* ===================== HEIGHT LABEL ===================== */ board.create('segment', [[R+1,0],[R+1,H]], {strokeWidth:2, strokeColor:'black', dash:1, fixed: true, highlight: false}); board.create('text', [R+1.5, H/2, "Height = {#h_p#} m"], {fixed: true, highlight: false}); /* ===================== RADIUS LABEL ===================== */ board.create('segment', [[0,H],[R,H]], {strokeWidth:2, strokeColor:'black', fixed: true, highlight: false}); board.create('text', [R/2, H+1, "Radius = {#r_p#} m"], {fixed: true, highlight: false}); /* ===================== TITLE LABEL ===================== */ board.create('text',[-4, H+R+2, "Prototype Tank"], {fixed: true, highlight: false}); [[/jsxgraph]]

Using the information above, answer the following. Give exact values where possible and round any decimal answers to 2 decimal places.

  1. Calculate the Area Scale Factor of the enlargement: [[input:ans1]] [[validation:ans1]] [[feedback:prt1]]
  2. Calculate the Volume Scale Factor of the enlargement: [[input:ans2]] [[validation:ans2]] [[feedback:prt2]]
  3. Calculate the exact volume of the prototype tank (cylindrical body + hemispherical top), giving your answer in \(\text{m}^3\) correct to 2 decimal places: [[input:ans3]] [[validation:ans3]] [[feedback:prt3]]
  4. Using your answer to part 3 and the Volume Scale Factor, calculate the volume of the industrial tank in \(\text{m}^3\), correct to 2 decimal places: [[input:ans4]] [[validation:ans4]] [[feedback:prt4]]

generalfeedback.text:
Worked Solution

When a solid is enlarged by a linear scale factor \(k\), lengths scale by \(k\), areas scale by \(k^2\), and volumes scale by \(k^3\). Here \(k = {@k@}\).

Part 1 — Area Scale Factor

Areas are two-dimensional, so they are enlarged by the square of the linear scale factor:

\[\text{Area Scale Factor} = k^2 = {@k@}^2 = {@ta1@}.\]

Part 2 — Volume Scale Factor

Volumes are three-dimensional, so they are enlarged by the cube of the linear scale factor:

\[\text{Volume Scale Factor} = k^3 = {@k@}^3 = {@ta2@}.\]

Part 3 — Volume of the prototype tank

The prototype is a cylinder of radius \(r = {@r_p@}\) m and height \(h = {@h_p@}\) m, topped by a hemisphere of radius \(r = {@r_p@}\) m. Its volume is the sum of the two:

\[V = \underbrace{\pi r^2 h}_{\text{cylinder}} + \underbrace{\tfrac{2}{3}\pi r^3}_{\text{hemisphere}}.\]

Substituting the prototype dimensions:

\[\begin{align} V &= \pi \times {@r_p@}^2 \times {@h_p@} \;+\; \tfrac{2}{3}\pi \times {@r_p@}^3 \\ &= {@dispVcyl@} \;+\; {@dispVhemi@} \\ &= {@ta3@} \text{ m}^3 \;\;(\text{to 2 d.p.}). \end{align}\]

Part 4 — Volume of the industrial tank

The industrial tank is the enlargement of the prototype, so multiply the prototype volume by the Volume Scale Factor:

\[\begin{align} V_{\text{industrial}} &= V_{\text{prototype}} \times k^3 \\ &= {@ta3@} \times {@ta2@} \\ &= {@ta4@} \text{ m}^3 \;\;(\text{to 2 d.p.}). \end{align}\]

prtcorrect.text: Correct answer, well done.

prtpartiallycorrect.text: Your answer is partially correct.

prtincorrect.text: Incorrect answer.

truefeedback.text: That is the linear scale factor \(k\). Area is two-dimensional, so it is enlarged by \(k^2\), not \(k\).
That is the volume scale factor \(k^3\). The area scale factor is \(k^2\).

falsefeedback.text: Not quite. The area scale factor is the square of the linear scale factor: \(k^2\).

truefeedback.text: That is the area scale factor \(k^2\). Volume is three-dimensional, so it is enlarged by \(k^3\).

falsefeedback.text: Not quite. The volume scale factor is the cube of the linear scale factor: \(k^3\).

truefeedback.text: You have found the volume of the cylindrical body only. Remember to add the volume of the hemispherical top, \(\tfrac{2}{3}\pi r^3\).

falsefeedback.text: Not quite. The prototype volume is the cylinder plus the hemisphere: \(\pi r^2 h + \tfrac{2}{3}\pi r^3\).

truefeedback.text: It looks like you multiplied by the area scale factor \(k^2\). To scale a volume, multiply by the volume scale factor \(k^3\).

falsefeedback.text: Not quite. Multiply your prototype volume from part 3 by the volume scale factor \(k^3\).
